\section[ruō, ruere]{ruō, ruere — to rush; to fall down}

\label{lesson:LA-C313-ruo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for exile, then the Latin for a chain.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ruō, ruere}
\textbf{ruō, ruere} — \textquotedblleft{}to rush; to fall down\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Aqua dē monte ruēbat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Water was rushing down from the mountain.}
\end{quote}

\emph{ruō, ruere, ruī, rutum}: any violent movement, forward or down.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ruō} is an inherited verb (EtymDB). English \emph{ruin} comes from its noun \emph{ruīna}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ruō, ruere}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ruō, ruere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ruō, ruere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for exile, then the Latin for a chain, then say \emph{ruō, ruere} again
\end{itemize}

\section[ruīna, ruīnae]{ruīna, ruīnae — a collapse, a fall; ruins}

\label{lesson:LA-C313-ruina}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a chain, then the Latin for to rush.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ruīna, ruīnae}
\textbf{ruīna, ruīnae} — \textquotedblleft{}a collapse, a fall; ruins\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Post ruīnam aedificiī nihil nisi saxa manēbat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After the collapse of the building nothing remained but stones.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, from \emph{ruō}. The plural \emph{ruīnae}: ruins. English \emph{ruin}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ruīna} is built on \emph{ruō}, \textquotedblleft{}to rush down, to collapse\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB): a falling down. English \emph{ruin} comes from it through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ruīna, ruīnae}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ruīna, ruīnae}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ruīna, ruīnae}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a chain, then the Latin for to rush, then say \emph{ruīna, ruīnae} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[corruō, corruere]{corruō, corruere — to collapse, to tumble down}

\label{lesson:LA-C313-corruo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to rush, then the Latin for a collapse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: corruō, corruere}
\textbf{corruō, corruere} — \textquotedblleft{}to collapse, to tumble down\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tabernae mihi duae corruērunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Two of my shops have tumbled down.}
\end{quote}

\emph{corruō, corruere, corruī}: \emph{con-} + \emph{ruō}. A landlord in one of Cicero's letters complains in these very words.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{corruō} is built on \emph{ruō}, \textquotedblleft{}to fall down\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{con-}, \textquotedblleft{}together, wholly\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to fall in a heap.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to rush, then the Latin for a collapse, then say \emph{corruō, corruere} again

\section[collābor, collābī]{collābor, collābī — to fall in, to collapse}

\label{lesson:LA-C313-collabor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a collapse, then the Latin for to collapse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: collābor, collābī}
\textbf{collābor, collābī} — \textquotedblleft{}to fall in, to collapse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Pōns vetus subitō collāpsus est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The old bridge suddenly collapsed.}
\end{quote}

\emph{collābor, collābī, collāpsus sum}, a deponent: \emph{con-} + \emph{lābor} (taught). English \emph{collapse} comes from its participle.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{collābor} is built on \emph{lābor}, \textquotedblleft{}to slip, to fall\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{con-} (Lewis \& Short): to fall together in ruins. English \emph{collapse} comes from its participle.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{collābor, collābī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{collābor, collābī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{collābor, collābī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a collapse, then the Latin for to collapse, then say \emph{collābor, collābī} again
\end{itemize}

\section[dēcidō, dēcidere]{dēcidō, dēcidere — to fall down, to fall off}

\label{lesson:LA-C313-decido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to collapse, then the Latin for to fall in.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dēcidō, dēcidere}
\textbf{dēcidō, dēcidere} — \textquotedblleft{}to fall down, to fall off\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tēgula dē tēctō dēcidit et ante mē frācta est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A tile fell off the roof and broke in front of me.}
\end{quote}

\emph{dēcidō, dēcidere, dēcidī}, short \emph{i}: \emph{dē} + \emph{cadō} (taught). Do not confuse \emph{dēcīdō}, 'to cut off'.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dēcidō} is built on \emph{cadō}, \textquotedblleft{}to fall\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{dē}, \textquotedblleft{}down from\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); the vowel changes inside the compound.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
